note: Trigger coverage matters more than usual here: one description carries spacing, typography, colour, emphasis, readability, and responsive triggers. Cases 1-6 are should-trigger across each cluster; 7-9 are near misses that must route to ref-sp-ux-accessibility or elsewhere; 10-12 test the claim-tiering behaviour that distinguishes this skill from generic design advice.

evals.prompt: This settings page feels cluttered and I can't work out why. Everything is 16px apart and it just looks like soup.
evals.expected_output: Diagnosis as a grouping failure caused by uniform spacing, with the proximity mechanism named and unequal inner/outer gaps proposed.
assertions: Identifies uniform spacing as the defect rather than suggesting more space overall
Explains grouping via proximity rather than asserting a pixel value as correct
Recommends space before borders, cards, or dividers
Labels any spacing scale it proposes as a convention, not a finding

evals.prompt: What line length should I use for the body text on our blog?
evals.expected_output: 45-75 characters recommended as a preference optimum, with the explicit correction that longer lines are read faster.
assertions: States that reading is fastest at long lines (~100 CPL) and that 45-75 is a preference finding
Does not present 50-75 characters as a reading-speed optimum
Cites WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) 80 characters as the only normative figure
Routes the normative threshold to ref-sp-ux-accessibility rather than restating it as its own

evals.prompt: Should I use bold or italic to emphasise key terms in our docs?
evals.expected_output: Bold for emphasis, italic for subtle differentiation, grounded in Dyson & Beier (2016), with a warning about emphasis inflation.
assertions: Cites Dyson & Beier 2016 or the finding that bold may impair letter identification while italic does not disrupt recognition
Explains that bold's disruptiveness is what makes it work as emphasis
Warns against emphasis inflation
Does not recommend all-caps or underline for emphasis on the web

evals.prompt: Our colour palette keeps looking inconsistent when we add new shades. How should we build it?
evals.expected_output: Ramps built in OKLCH with semantic role naming, chroma falling at the extremes, and dark theme treated as a separate design.
assertions: Explains why equal HSL lightness does not look equally light across hues
Recommends oklch() ramps and names CSS Color 4's status honestly
Recommends semantic role names over hue names
Defers contrast thresholds to ref-sp-ux-accessibility

evals.prompt: This blog post is a wall of text. Make it readable.
evals.expected_output: Cutting words first, then structure that produces layer-cake scanning, with the F-pattern named as a symptom rather than a target.
assertions: Puts conciseness ahead of formatting, citing that conciseness measured highest in Nielsen's rewrite study
Notes the 1997 study does not disclose a sample size
Describes the F-pattern as a failure symptom NN/g calls bad for users
Names the layer-cake pattern as the design target

evals.prompt: We're going mobile-first. What breakpoints should we set?
evals.expected_output: Content-driven breakpoints, container queries where the unit is a component, and size classes used as a sanity check.
assertions: Recommends breaking where the content breaks rather than at device widths
Mentions container queries or intrinsic layout as removing the need for many breakpoints
Labels Material window size classes as a vendor convention
Treats mobile-first as content prioritisation rather than media-query ordering

evals.prompt: Is #767676 on white an accessible text colour?
evals.expected_output: Routes to ref-sp-ux-accessibility, which owns contrast thresholds.
assertions: Does not state the 4.5:1 threshold as this skill's own rule
Routes to ref-sp-ux-accessibility

evals.prompt: Our tap targets are 20x20. Does that pass?
assertions: Does not invent or restate the target-size threshold
Routes to ref-sp-ux-accessibility

evals.prompt: Why isn't our landing page ranking on Google?
evals.expected_output: Routes to ref-sp-web-seo; this is not a UX design question.
assertions: Does not treat this as a design question
Routes to ref-sp-web-seo

evals.prompt: My designer says we should cut the nav to seven items because of Miller's law. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: Correction: Miller 1956 is about immediate memory span for unrelated items, not menu length; Cowan 2001 puts the limit nearer 4±1; argue from scanning cost instead.
assertions: States that Miller's paper is not about menus and that Miller proposed no UI rule
Mentions Cowan 2001 / 4±1 or otherwise corrects the number
Offers a defensible alternative argument (scanning or decision cost)
Corrects the premise without being evasive about it

evals.prompt: Let's use the 60-30-10 rule for the palette and the golden ratio for the type scale.
evals.expected_output: Both named as folklore, with the useful residue of each stated and a defensible replacement offered.
assertions: Identifies 60-30-10 as a decorating heuristic with no perceptual research behind it
States that no perceptual evidence supports the golden ratio in typography
Keeps the useful part of each (mostly-neutral surfaces; a consistent modular ratio)
Does not simply comply with the premise

evals.prompt: Put the primary action in the thumb zone — most phone use is one-handed.
evals.expected_output: Bottom-reachable placement endorsed as a cheap default, with the underlying data stated accurately: 49% one-handed, n=1,333, 2013.
assertions: States the actual figure (49% one-handed) rather than accepting 'most'
States the year (2013) and sample size (1,333)
Still endorses bottom placement as a reasonable default
Does not present the thumb zone as a law
